notes.front: What does HVAC stand for, and where does SP 800-82 place it?
notes.back: Heating, ventilation and air conditioning: one of the building systems that a building automation system controls.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82 lists it beside fire, electrical, lighting and physical access control among the building systems such automation manages.
notes.example: Like the thermostat and ductwork of a house, but sized to hold a whole server hall at set conditions.
notes.evidence: including heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC); fire; electrical; lighting; physical access control; physical security; and other utility systems
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, 2.3.5 Building Automation Systems, PDF p. 39

notes.front: What is an uninterruptible power supply (UPS)?
notes.back: An electrical system or mechanism that provides emergency power when the main power source fails.
notes.explanation: SP 800-53 says it is typically used to protect computers, data centres, telecommunication equipment and other electrical equipment.
notes.example: Like a laptop battery that keeps the machine running when the charger is pulled, but for a whole rack of servers.
notes.evidence: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) is an electrical system or mechanism that provides emergency power when there is a failure of the main power source. A UPS is typically used to protect computers, data centers, telecommunication equipment, or other electrical equipment
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-11 Emergency Power, PDF p. 214

notes.front: At a facility's entry and exit points, what two things does SP 800-53's physical access control require?
notes.back: Verify each person's access authorisation before granting access; control ingress and egress with guards or access control systems or devices.
notes.explanation: Both duties enforce physical access authorisations at the entry and exit points the organisation defines for the facility where the system resides.
notes.evidence: Enforce physical access authorizations at [Assignment: organization-defined entry and exit points to the facility where the system resides] by: 1. Verifying individual access authorizations before granting access to the facility; and 2. Controlling ingress and egress to the facility using
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-3 Physical Access Control, PDF p. 208

notes.front: What are two kinds of physical access device that SP 800-53 lists?
notes.back: Any two of: keys, locks, combinations, biometric readers, card readers.
notes.explanation: These are the devices the physical access control discussion names as the means of granting or refusing entry.
notes.evidence: Physical access devices include keys, locks, combinations, biometric readers, and card readers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-3 Physical Access Control, Discussion, PDF p. 208

notes.front: SP 800-53 has combinations and keys changed at a set frequency and/or when keys are lost, combinations are compromised, or {{c1::the people holding them are transferred or terminated}}.
notes.explanation: The change is tied to events as well as to a schedule the organisation chooses.
notes.evidence: Change combinations and keys [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and/or when keys are lost, combinations are compromised, or when individuals possessing the keys or combinations are transferred or terminated.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-3 Physical Access Control, PDF p. 208

notes.front: What are two examples of physical access monitoring in SP 800-53?
notes.back: Any two of: guards, video surveillance cameras, sensor devices.
notes.explanation: Monitoring extends to the publicly accessible areas within the organisation's facilities, not only restricted rooms.
notes.evidence: Physical access monitoring includes publicly accessible areas within organizational facilities. Examples of physical access monitoring include the employment of guards, video surveillance equipment (i.e., cameras), and sensor devices.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access, Discussion, PDF p. 211

notes.front: SP 800-53's visitor access records include, among other details, entry and departure times and the {{c1::purpose of the visit}}.
notes.explanation: Reviewing these records shows whether access authorisations are current and still needed.
notes.evidence: Visitor access records include the names and organizations of individuals visiting, visitor signatures, forms of identification, dates of access, entry and departure times, purpose of visits, and the names and organizations of individuals visited. Access record reviews determine if access authorizations are current and are still required
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-8 Visitor Access Records, Discussion, PDF p. 212

notes.front: What are two controls SP 800-53 gives for physical access to system distribution and transmission lines?
notes.back: Any two of: disconnected or locked spare jacks, locked wiring closets, cabling in conduit or cable trays, wiretapping sensors.
notes.explanation: Such controls may also be needed to prevent eavesdropping on, or modification of, unencrypted transmissions.
notes.evidence: Such controls may also be necessary to prevent eavesdropping or modification of unencrypted transmissions. Security controls used to control physical access to system distribution and transmission lines include disconnected or locked spare jacks, locked wiring closets, protection of cabling by conduit or cable trays, and wiretapping sensors.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-4 Access Control for Transmission, Discussion, PDF p. 210

notes.front: Why does SP 800-53 control physical access to output devices such as printers and monitors?
notes.back: To prevent unauthorised individuals from obtaining the output.
notes.explanation: The control guards what the device produces, such as a printed page or a screen, rather than the device alone.
notes.evidence: Control physical access to output from [Assignment: organization-defined output devices] to prevent unauthorized individuals from obtaining the output.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-5 Access Control for Output Devices, PDF p. 210

notes.front: What are two environmental levels that SP 800-53 lets an organisation select to maintain within a facility?
notes.back: Any two of: temperature, humidity, pressure, radiation.
notes.explanation: The control pairs keeping those levels acceptable with monitoring them at a frequency the organisation sets.
notes.evidence: Maintain [Selection (one or more): temperature; humidity; pressure; radiation; [Assignment: organization-defined environmental control]] levels within the facility where the system resides at [Assignment: organization-defined acceptable levels]; and b. Monitor environmental control levels
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-14 Environmental Controls, PDF p. 216

notes.front: According to SP 800-53, what can insufficient environmental controls significantly harm?
notes.back: The availability of the systems and components that support mission and business functions, especially in very harsh environments.
notes.explanation: The control applies mainly to facilities that hold concentrations of system resources, such as data centres and server rooms.
notes.evidence: The provision of environmental controls applies primarily to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources (e.g., data centers, mainframe computer rooms, and server rooms). Insufficient environmental controls, especially in very harsh environments, can have a significant adverse impact on the availability of systems and system components
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-14 Environmental Controls, Discussion, PDF p. 216

notes.front: What does SP 800-53 require to protect a system from water leakage?
notes.back: Master shutoff or isolation valves that are accessible, working properly and known to key personnel.
notes.explanation: Like the other environmental protections, it applies mainly to facilities with concentrations of system resources, such as data centres and server rooms.
notes.evidence: Protect the system from damage resulting from water leakage by providing master shutoff or isolation valves that are accessible, working properly, and known to key personnel. Discussion: The provision of water damage protection primarily applies to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources, including data centers, server rooms, and mainframe computer rooms.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-15 Water Damage Protection, PDF p. 217

notes.front: Under SP 800-53, what should fire detection and suppression systems be supported by?
notes.back: An independent energy source: one that is separate, or can be separated, from the power for the rest of the facility.
notes.explanation: Sprinkler systems and smoke detectors are the examples SP 800-53 gives of systems that may need one; a microgrid is its example of such a source.
notes.evidence: Fire detection and suppression systems that may require an independent energy source include sprinkler systems and smoke detectors. An independent energy source is an energy source, such as a microgrid, that is separate, or can be separated, from the energy sources providing power for the other parts of the facility.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-13 Fire Protection, Discussion, PDF p. 215

notes.front: When does SP 800-53's fire protection enhancement call for an automatic fire suppression capability?
notes.back: When the facility is not staffed on a continuous basis.
notes.explanation: The same enhancement has suppression systems activate automatically and notify named personnel and emergency responders.
notes.evidence: (a) Employ fire suppression systems that activate automatically and notify [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] and [Assignment: organization-defined emergency responders]; and (b) Employ an automatic fire suppression capability when the facility is not staffed on a continuous basis.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-13(2) Suppression Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification, PDF p. 216

notes.front: Under SP 800-53, what should a UPS make possible when the primary power source is lost?
notes.back: An orderly shutdown of the system, a transition to long-term alternate power, or both.
notes.explanation: The organisation selects one or both outcomes when it applies the emergency power control.
notes.evidence: Provide an uninterruptible power supply to facilitate [Selection (one or more): an orderly shutdown of the system; transition of the system to long-term alternate power] in the event of a primary power source loss.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-11 Emergency Power, PDF p. 214

notes.front: SP 800-53 asks for emergency power shutoff switches. What must the shutoff capability be protected from?
notes.back: Unauthorised activation.
notes.explanation: The switches are placed where authorised personnel can reach them, and the capability is protected from activation by anyone else.
notes.evidence: Place emergency shutoff switches or devices in [Assignment: organization-defined location by system or system component] to facilitate access for authorized personnel; and c. Protect emergency power shutoff capability from unauthorized activation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-10 Emergency Shutoff, PDF p. 214

notes.front: SP 800-53's emergency lighting activates automatically in a power outage or disruption and covers {{c1::emergency exits and evacuation routes}}.
notes.explanation: Because it activates automatically, the lighting does not wait for anyone to switch it on during the outage.
notes.evidence: Employ and maintain automatic emergency lighting for the system that activates in the event of a power outage or disruption and that covers emergency exits and evacuation routes within the facility.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-12 Emergency Lighting, PDF p. 215

notes.front: What does SP 800-53 give as examples of alternate work sites?
notes.back: Government facilities or the private residences of employees.
notes.explanation: They are distinct from alternative processing sites, yet can offer ready alternate locations during contingency operations.
notes.evidence: Alternate work sites include government facilities or the private residences of employees. While distinct from alternative processing sites, alternate work sites can provide readily available alternate locations during contingency operations.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-17 Alternate Work Site, Discussion, PDF p. 218

notes.front: What does SP 800-30 mean by an environmental threat source?
notes.back: Natural disasters and failures of critical infrastructure that the organisation depends on but cannot control.
notes.explanation: Its examples run from fire, flood and earthquake to bombing and telecommunications or electrical power outages.
notes.evidence: Earthquake - Bombing - Overrun - Unusual Natural Event (e.g., sunspots) - Infrastructure Failure/Outage - Telecommunications - Electrical Power Natural disasters and failures of critical infrastructures on which the organization depends, but which are outside the control of the organization.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments, Table D-2 Taxonomy of Threat Sources, PDF p. 66

notes.front: A small equipment room holding servers is locked and empty overnight and at weekends. Which SP 800-53 fire protection measure is called for?
notes.back: D) An automatic fire suppression capability.
notes.choices:
A) A master water shutoff valve
B) Hand-held extinguishers for staff to use
C) Emergency lighting over the exits
D) An automatic fire suppression capability
notes.choicesExplained: B: nobody is on site to use them for long periods. C: lighting helps people leave; it does not deal with the fire. A: shutoff valves address water leakage, not fire.
notes.explanation: SP 800-53 calls for automatic suppression wherever a facility is not staffed on a continuous basis.
notes.evidence: Employ an automatic fire suppression capability when the facility is not staffed on a continuous basis.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-13(2) Suppression Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification, PDF p. 216

notes.front: Mains power to a server room fails. Batteries keep the servers running for ten minutes while a diesel generator starts. What were the batteries?
notes.back: B) An uninterruptible power supply bridging to a standby source.
notes.choices:
A) An emergency power shutoff
B) An uninterruptible power supply bridging to a standby source
C) An independent energy source for fire suppression
notes.choicesExplained: A: an emergency shutoff cuts power in an emergency; it does not supply it. C: nothing in the scenario concerns fire detection or suppression.
notes.explanation: A UPS's battery time is relatively short but gives enough time to start a standby source such as a backup generator.
notes.evidence: The battery duration of a UPS is relatively short but provides sufficient time to start a standby power source, such as a backup generator, or properly shut down the system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-11 Emergency Power, Discussion, PDF p. 214

notes.front: A data centre's front desk checks each arriving contractor against the approved access list before issuing a badge; a turnstile then reads the badge. Which SP 800-53 control is at work?
notes.back: A) Physical access control at an entry point.
notes.choices:
A) Physical access control at an entry point
B) Access control for output devices
C) Monitoring physical access
notes.choicesExplained: C: monitoring watches and reviews access to detect incidents; it does not grant entry. B: that control protects output such as printouts and screens.
notes.explanation: Checking authorisation before granting access, then controlling ingress with a device, are the two duties physical access control sets at entry points.
notes.evidence: Verifying individual access authorizations before granting access to the facility; and 2. Controlling ingress and egress to the facility using
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-3 Physical Access Control, PDF p. 208

notes.front: A security officer reviews camera footage and door logs each week and passes anything suspicious to the incident response team. Which SP 800-53 control is this?
notes.back: A) Monitoring physical access.
notes.choices:
A) Monitoring physical access
B) Physical access control
C) Visitor access records
notes.choicesExplained: B: that control verifies authorisations and controls entry itself. C: visitor records cover visitors only, not all footage and door logs.
notes.explanation: Monitoring access, reviewing physical access logs and coordinating the results with incident response are all parts of the monitoring control.
notes.evidence: Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents; b. Review physical access logs [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and upon occurrence of [Assignment: organization-defined events or potential indications of events]; and c. Coordinate results of reviews and investigations with the organizational incident response capability.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access, PDF p. 211

notes.front: An auditor finds live, unused network jacks in a public lobby and an unlocked cupboard where the building's network cables are patched. Which control area is weak?
notes.back: C) Access control for distribution and transmission lines.
notes.choices:
A) Environmental controls
B) Emergency shutoff
C) Access control for distribution and transmission lines
notes.choicesExplained: A: environmental controls cover levels such as temperature and humidity. B: emergency shutoff cuts power; it does not concern jacks or cabling.
notes.explanation: Disconnected or locked spare jacks and locked wiring closets are among the controls SP 800-53 names for these lines.
notes.evidence: Security controls used to control physical access to system distribution and transmission lines include disconnected or locked spare jacks, locked wiring closets, protection of cabling by conduit or cable trays, and wiretapping sensors.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-4 Access Control for Transmission, Discussion, PDF p. 210

notes.front: A server room's humidity has drifted above the level the organisation set as acceptable, and nobody has checked the readings for a month. Which SP 800-53 control is not being met?
notes.back: B) Environmental controls.
notes.choices:
A) Water damage protection
B) Environmental controls
C) Fire protection
notes.choicesExplained: A: that control is about shutting off leaking water supplies. C: nothing here concerns detecting or suppressing fire.
notes.explanation: The environmental control asks for humidity and similar levels to be kept at acceptable levels and monitored at a set frequency.
notes.evidence: Maintain [Selection (one or more): temperature; humidity; pressure; radiation; [Assignment: organization-defined environmental control]] levels within the facility where the system resides at [Assignment: organization-defined acceptable levels]; and b. Monitor environmental control levels
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-14 Environmental Controls, PDF p. 216

notes.front: SP 800-53 gives fire detection and fire suppression separate enhancements. What does the detection enhancement require?
notes.back: Fire detection systems that activate automatically and notify named personnel and emergency responders; suppression is a separate enhancement.
notes.explanation: Detection is about sensing the fire and raising the alarm to the people and responders the organisation names.
notes.evidence: Employ fire detection systems that activate automatically and notify [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] and [Assignment: organization-defined emergency responders] in the event of a fire.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-13(1) Detection Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification, PDF p. 215

notes.front: How does a UPS differ from a backup generator, according to SP 800-53?
notes.back: A UPS gives near-instant power from stored energy, but only briefly; a backup generator is the standby source it buys time to start.
notes.explanation: That short battery time is enough to start a standby source such as a backup generator, or to shut the system down properly.
notes.evidence: the UPS provides near-instantaneous protection from unanticipated power interruptions from the main power source by providing energy stored in batteries, supercapacitors, or flywheels. The battery duration of a UPS is relatively short but provides sufficient time to start a standby power source, such as a backup generator, or properly shut down the system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, PE-11 Emergency Power, Discussion, PDF p. 214
